works.abstract: ABSTRACT California’s Central Valley, a major agricultural region in North America, relies on river systems to support farming. Anthropogenic activities produce pollutants that present substantial risks to aquatic systems and the broader environment. The Central Valley is recognized as a global leader in agriculture; however, baseline data on microplastics (MPs) in its major rivers are limited. This study quantifies the abundance and chemical composition of MPs in water and sediment from the Stanislaus, Tuolumne, Merced, and San Joaquin rivers. MPs were extracted using the density separation procedure with NaCl, followed by oxidation of the organic material with H 2 O 2 , and then quantified for abundance, morphotypes, and size range under a stereo microscope. All samples tested positive; MPs’ range and mean ± SE were 85–210 (148.42 ± 11.51) items/L in water and 292–712 (507.33 ± 39.53) items/kg in sediment samples. Fiber was the dominant morphotype, with most items measuring < 2.5 mm. ATR-FTIR spectroscopy analysis revealed the presence of nine polymers, with the majority being cellophane and polyethylene. The potential uptake of MPs by edible crops through irrigation with river water, as well as by aquatic fauna and water recreationists highlights the urgent need for effective mitigation strategies. These findings establish a baseline for future monitoring of riverine MPs in California's Central Valley. They also identify potential pathways for MPs to enter agricultural and aquatic ecosystems, thereby providing information relevant to environmental management and mitigation efforts.
works.title: Riverine microplastic pollution in the agriculturally rich Central Valley, California, USA
